title: What Are EMIs and How Do They Work?
summary: What an EMI is, how the formula works with rupee figures, flat versus reducing rates, what happens when rates change and what a missed EMI costs.
body_markdown:
EMI stands for equated monthly instalment. It is the same amount you pay a lender every month until a loan is repaid. Each EMI covers that month's interest and repays a part of the amount you borrowed, so the last instalment clears the loan.


## What is an EMI?


An EMI is one fixed monthly payment that covers the interest for that month and a slice of the loan itself. Home loans, car loans, personal loans and education loans work this way. So can a credit card purchase converted into EMIs.


Three terms come up again and again:


- **Principal** is the amount you borrow.
- **Interest rate** is what the lender charges for lending it, shown as a percentage for a year.
- **Tenure** is how long you take to repay, counted in months.


## How does an EMI work?


The amount borrowed, the interest rate and the tenure together set the EMI. Each month the lender charges interest only on what you still owe, and the rest of your EMI reduces that balance.


That is the reducing balance method. The amount you still owe at any point is the outstanding balance, and the interest falls as it does.


A longer tenure gives a smaller EMI but more interest in total. A shorter tenure does the opposite.


## How is an EMI calculated?


A reducing-balance EMI uses one formula: EMI = P × R × (1 + R)^N ÷ \[(1 + R)^N − 1\]. P is the loan amount, R is the monthly interest rate written as a decimal, and N is the number of monthly instalments. To get R, divide the yearly rate by 12.


Take Arjun, who borrows ₹5,00,000 for 5 years at an assumed 11% a year. R is 0.11 ÷ 12, about 0.009167, and N is 60. The formula gives an EMI of ₹10,871 a month, rounded to the rupee.


Over 60 months he repays ₹6,52,260, so ₹1,52,260 is interest. In his first month, the interest is ₹4,583 and the other ₹6,288 of the EMI repays the loan. You can check any loan of your own on the[personal loan calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/personal-loan-calculator) , the[home loan calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/home-loan-calculator) or the[car loan calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/car-loan-calculator) . All three use this formula and round the EMI to the rupee.


Before you sign, the lender must also hand you a Key Facts Statement. For retail term loans sanctioned on or after 1 October 2024, RBI requires it. It shows the EMI and the full repayment schedule over the loan's life.


## Flat rate or reducing balance: why do two loans at the same rate cost differently?


A flat rate charges interest on the full loan amount for the whole tenure, so it costs more than the same rate on a reducing balance. On a reducing balance the interest shrinks as you repay. On a flat rate it never does.


Here is Arjun's loan again, with both methods at an assumed 11% for 5 years:


Method (assumed 11% a year) Monthly EMI Total interest


Reducing balance ₹10,871 ₹1,52,260


Flat rate ₹12,917 ₹2,75,000


The flat figure is simple: 11% of ₹5,00,000 is ₹55,000 a year, which is ₹2,75,000 over 5 years.


That makes the flat loan cost about the same as 18.8% a year on a reducing balance. The 18.8% is worked the way RBI works out the annual percentage rate (the monthly rate multiplied by 12, with no fees in this example).


The annual percentage rate, or APR, is the yearly cost of a loan including its fees. The Key Facts Statement carries it, so offers using different methods can be compared on one number.


## Why is the interest share of an EMI highest at the start?


Interest is charged on the balance still owed, and that balance is largest in month one. So each EMI starts with the biggest interest share, and the share shrinks as the balance falls.


This steady paying down of the balance is called amortisation, and a table that shows it month by month is an amortisation schedule. Here is Arjun's loan, year by year, at the assumed 11%:


Year Interest paid Principal repaid Balance at year end


1 ₹51,077 ₹79,377 ₹4,20,623


2 ₹41,892 ₹88,563 ₹3,32,060


3 ₹31,643 ₹98,811 ₹2,33,249


4 ₹20,209 ₹1,10,246 ₹1,23,003


5 ₹7,452 ₹1,23,003 ₹0


These figures use the exact EMI before rounding, so total interest here is ₹1,52,273, a little above the calculator's ₹1,52,260.


On this assumed loan, a third of all the interest falls in year 1. After 30 EMIs, ₹2,84,006 is still owed, which is more than half of the original loan.


A shorter loan works the same way. On ₹1,00,000 at an assumed 12% for 12 months, the first EMI of ₹8,885 holds ₹1,000 of interest and the last only ₹88.


## What happens to your EMI when interest rates change?


On a fixed-rate loan the EMI stays the same. On a floating-rate loan the rate moves with a benchmark, so either the EMI or the tenure changes. The word "fixed" needs care, because RBI calls a loan fixed-rate only if the rate stays the same for the whole term. Some home loans sold as fixed are fixed for a few years and then turn floating.


A bank's floating-rate loan is tied to an external benchmark, a published reference rate. RBI's list includes its policy repo rate, and the three-month and six-month Treasury Bill yields published by the Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd. The loan's rate must be reset at least once in three months. A reset means the rate is recalculated against the benchmark.


The repo rate is the rate RBI's Monetary Policy Committee sets to reach its inflation target. RBI's Current Rates panel showed a policy repo rate of 5.25% as at 1 October 2026.


When the repo rate rises or falls, a loan tied to it follows at the next reset. The bank's margin over the benchmark is the spread. RBI's rule says the part of the spread for credit risk can change only when your credit assessment changes substantially. Other parts of the spread can be altered once in three years.


Housing finance companies set floating rates by their own interest rate model instead, so check what your loan is linked to.


### A worked example of a rate rise


Sunita has a floating-rate home loan of ₹20,00,000 over 15 years at an assumed 8.5% a year. Her EMI is ₹19,695. After 36 EMIs she owes ₹17,74,217.


Suppose, as an assumption and not a forecast, the rate rises to 9% at a reset. Two of her choices are:


- Keep the end date and pay a higher EMI of ₹20,191, which is ₹496 more.
- Keep the EMI at ₹19,695 and take 7 more months, with 151 EMIs left instead of 144.


From that point the interest is ₹11,33,306 with the higher EMI and ₹11,93,473 with the longer tenure, about ₹60,167 more.


### What the lender must tell you and offer


When your floating rate goes up, the lender must tell you how it changes your EMI or tenure. Any increase must be communicated to you immediately. The rule covers banks, NBFCs and housing finance companies alike.


You must be allowed to choose a higher EMI, a longer tenure, a mix of the two, or prepaying part or all of the loan. Prepaying means paying back money before the schedule says so.


The lender may also offer a switch to a fixed rate, with any charge stated upfront. A longer tenure cannot be stretched so far that your loan balance grows. Every quarter you should get a statement showing what you have repaid, the EMIs left and the annual rate.


## What kinds of EMI are there?


EMIs differ mainly by the rate behind them, fixed or floating, and by how the loan is paid out. These are the ones you will meet:


- **Fixed-rate EMI.** The rate stays the same for the whole tenure, which is RBI's meaning of fixed for banks.
- **Floating-rate EMI.** The rate follows a benchmark, as above, and the EMI or tenure moves with it.
- **Pre-EMI.** This arises on a home that is still being built. The lender pays the builder in stages as construction reaches each one, not all at once. While the home is being built, interest is charged only on the amount released to the builder. SBI describes its Pre-EMI option (read October 2026) the same way, with the actual EMI starting after possession of the house. See[how to apply for a home loan](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-apply-for-a-home-loan) .
- **Card EMI and no-cost EMI.** A credit card purchase can be converted into EMIs. A no-cost EMI is one made "no cost" by an upfront discount from the merchant or card issuer. RBI requires the bank to show the principal, interest and any such discount before you convert, and again on the statement. An EMI that carries interest may not be called no-cost. See[personal loan or credit card](https://koshex.com/blog/choosing-between-a-personal-loan-and-a-credit-card) .


## What happens if you miss an EMI?


The loan is overdue from the due date, the lender may add a penal charge, and the missed payment can reach the credit bureaus. An EMI bounce is the plain version: the automatic debit for your EMI failed.


A penal charge is a late-payment charge. RBI's rules say it is charged on the overdue amount and disclosed in your loan agreement and Key Facts Statement. It cannot be extra interest added to your rate, and no interest can be charged on the penalty itself. Interest keeps running on the unpaid EMI at your normal loan rate.


SBI's personal loan page (updated 6 May 2026) lists 2.40% a year on the irregular portion for up to 60 days, and 5% a year beyond 60 days. Those are SBI's figures, not a rule for every lender.


Meanwhile the loan moves through stages. Banks tag it as an early-stress account at once and, after 30 and 60 days unpaid, at higher stress levels. If instalments stay unpaid for more than 90 days, the loan becomes a non-performing asset (NPA) in the bank's books, which shows on your credit report.


Lenders report loan accounts to the credit bureaus as on the 9th, 16th, 23rd and last day of each month. That includes accounts where only the number of days overdue has changed. The lender must also alert you by SMS or email when it reports a default.


For the score side, see[why your CIBIL score may be low](https://koshex.com/blog/reasons-for-having-a-low-cibil-score-how-to-improve-it) . If instalments are out of reach, see[how to get out of a debt trap](https://koshex.com/blog/5-steps-to-get-out-of-a-debt-trap) .


## How much EMI can you afford?


There is no single rule. The answer depends on your take-home pay, the EMIs you already pay, your essential costs and the cash you keep aside. Lenders set their own limits. For the cash you keep aside, see[where to keep your emergency savings](https://koshex.com/blog/where-should-you-keep-your-emergency-savings) . For home loans, see[home loan EMI and affordability](https://koshex.com/blog/home-loan-emi-calculate-the-right-amount-with-the-home-loan-emi-calculator) .


Later, you may want to repay early. Say your loan is on a floating rate and you took it as an individual for a purpose other than business. The lender cannot charge you for prepaying it. A home loan and a personal loan are examples. This holds for part or full prepayment, from any source of money and at any time.


On a fixed-rate loan the lender may charge what its policy and your loan papers say, worked out on the amount you prepay. Check which kind of rate your loan has before you assume either.[Methods to pay your home loan faster](https://koshex.com/blog/methods-to-pay-your-home-loan-faster) covers prepayment in detail.
